items.text: SEASON 8 · EPISODE 8 · DRAFT  The main hall and the stage-left rack · Maya, Dario, Nkechi and Marshal Lindqvist · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  The fire marshal pulled a station on her walkthrough. The evacuation message played — with the program music still playing under it.  ⚑ RV-163: the fire alarm system is the fire alarm contractor’s and its acceptance the marshal’s; nothing in a life-safety interface is ever jumpered, bypassed or disabled. RV-161: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: The Relay
items.stakes: The fire marshal pulled a station and heard music under the evacuation message. No pass, no occupancy.
items.reward: An interface that mutes when it should, fails safe when it breaks, and can't be ‘tidied’ out of existence.

objectives.text: Decide what you tell the marshal
Find where the mute got lost
Decide what protects it next time
Look closer: two things in the rack

items.rumor: The safest wire is the one that shouts when it's cut.

items.alt: The main hall; the fire alarm panel shows ALARM; musical notes drift from the ceiling; Marshal Lindqvist points up; Maya stares.

bubbles.text: Evacuation message — and music under it. Why?

items.caption: No pass, no occupancy.

lines.text: I'll be back Friday at ten. If your music plays under my message, there's no occupancy.
Understood. You'll have evidence before you have my word.

items.prompt: 10:05. The marshal has stopped the test. What do you tell her?
items.risk: An unoccupiable building on opening week — or a hidden fault in a life-safety system.

hints.text: Whose side of the interface do you start on — and who touches it?

options.label: Show her the commissioning record — the interface passed three weeks ago
options.result: Marshal Lindqvist: “That's paper. I just heard music.”

options.label: “It failed. We'll find out why and show you the evidence before Friday.” Then: the fire alarm contractor confirms the relay; Dario's tech traces the wiring at the rack; nobody but the fire alarm contractor touches their side
options.consequence: Own the failure; follow the signal; stay on your side of the line.

options.label: Program the DSP to mute when it hears the evacuation message instead
options.result: A redesign of a life-safety interface, by the wrong person, in a morning.
options.consequence: The sequence is the fire alarm designer's.
options.fail: The sequence belongs to the fire alarm designer.

options.label: Turn the program audio off until opening
options.result: Silence isn't a fix; opening night the fault is still there.

items.title: The jumper.
items.body: The fire alarm contractor's meter: relay K3 opens in alarm, exactly as designed. At the stage-left rack, Dario's tech finds the relay pair on logic input 7 — and a short jumper across input 3, the input the DSP watches, tagged ‘TEMP — punch 188’. Punch 188 said ‘tidy logic terminal strip’. Moving the pair left input 3 open; the interface is normally closed, so open means alarm and the program muted all day. The fail-safe worked. Then someone ‘fixed’ it.
items.label: Test: how long did the music play — and why was it silent?

items.label: **Find it:** where did the mute get lost?

items.alt: An interface sheet before the fix: pull station, fire alarm panel and relay K3 — the fire alarm contractor's — in red; DSP logic input 3 and program mute — the AV contractor's — in blue; the link into the DSP is broken: input 3 jumpered, the relay on input 7, from punch 188 ‘tidy terminal strip’; a mute-time bar of relay 0.05 s, scan 0.1 s and ramp 0.5 s totalling 0.65 s against a 2 s line; the record says PASS, three weeks before punch 188.
items.caption: The design was right. The rack wasn't.

items.text: Act II — “Every change re-opens the test”

items.title: Every change re-opens the test.
items.body: Nkechi lays two papers side by side: the interface test, PASS, 0.7 s, witnessed — and punch 188, closed nineteen days later. Nothing connected them. The punch list didn't know the rack held a life-safety interface, and the tech didn't either. On paper it still passes. In the hall it plays music.
items.label: Test: the margin — and why the PASS doesn't count.

items.risk: A fix nobody can prove on Friday.
timeout: Thursday's test runs out of time.

hints.text: What would you show the marshal besides your word?

options.label: Dario's tech moves it back tonight; the record already says PASS
options.result: No witness, no timing, and the same record that was wrong this morning.

options.label: Dario's tech re-lands the pair on input 3 per the as-built and removes the jumper, with the fire alarm contractor witnessing; then an end-to-end test — the fire alarm contractor at the panel, Nkechi timing — before the marshal returns
options.result: Pair on input 3, jumper bagged, program mutes 0.7 s after the relay opens.
options.consequence: Back to the design, witnessed and timed.

options.label: Leave the jumper and point the DSP at input 7
options.result: It mutes — and the drawings, the DSP file and the rack now disagree.

options.label: Ask the fire alarm contractor to move their relay closer
options.result: Their relay was never the problem.

items.title: The telegraph that rang the bells
items.body: In 1852 Boston switched on the first city-wide fire-alarm telegraph, designed by William Channing and Moses Farmer. Turning the crank in a street box sent the box's number down a wire to a central office, and from there the alarm was struck on bells across the city. For the first time, news of a fire travelled faster than a runner — and every box had to work every time, so they were tested.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #79 · AVERY'S LENS  A safety interface fails safe — and stays tested  Design life-safety interfaces so a fault is loud (a cut wire mutes), and treat every change near them as a reason to test again.  The interface was designed to fail safe. A tidy-up broke it, the fail-safe muted the program, and a jumper ‘fixed’ the mute — silently removing the safety.

items.alt: The interface sheet after the fix: the whole chain green, from pull station to program mute; relay pair on logic input 3, jumper removed, terminals labelled; the mute time of 0.65 s well inside the 2 s line; the marshal's retest PASS, and any change to this rack re-opens the test.
items.caption: Muted in under a second — and harder to break.

items.prompt: My tech thought he was helping. The program kept muting and the painters were complaining. Do I let him go?

options.label: “He fixed the symptom he could see. The gap is ours: nobody told him that rack holds a life-safety interface. Label it, train him, keep him.”
options.reply: He'll be the one who never touches it again. And he'll tell the others.

options.label: “That's your call.”
options.reply: It is. I was asking what you'd do.

options.label: “Yes. That can't happen.”
options.reply: And the next tech won't know either.

items.title: TEMP — punch 188
items.body: A three-centimetre jumper across logic input 3, with a paper tag in marker: ‘TEMP — punch 188 — prog kept muting’. Two weeks old. It held the safety input closed for every alarm since.

items.prompt: Friday, after the marshal signs. What protects the interface from the next tidy-up?
known: ◉ Punch list blind to life safety
items.risk: The same fault after the next tidy-up.

hints.text: How would the next tech know?

options.label: A stern email
options.result: Read once, forgotten by the next crew.

options.label: Terminals labelled LIFE SAFETY — DO NOT RE-PATCH; the DSP's logic page locked and documented; any punch item touching that rack flagged and followed by a re-test with the fire alarm contractor
options.result: Nkechi writes the rule into the commissioning plan; Dario briefs every tech.
options.consequence: Make the safe thing obvious and the change visible.

options.label: Padlock the rack for ever
options.result: Nobody can maintain anything in it.
options.consequence: Safe until the first real fault.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the two days yourself.

items.alt: The main hall during the retest; the panel in ALARM; no music notes this time; Marshal Lindqvist nods; Nkechi holds a stopwatch.

bubbles.text: Just my message. Good. Now do it for the whole building on opening day.

items.title: Interface test · PASS
items.body: The commissioning record: ‘Sequence item 7 — program mute on alarm — PASS — 0.7 s — witnessed.’ Dated nineteen days before punch 188 was closed. No link between the two.

items.alt: The site trailer; the punch list printed on a long roll across the table; Nkechi points at a number; Maya reads it.

bubbles.text: Four hundred and twelve open items. Nineteen working days. And sixty that say ‘closed’ I've never seen.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  The sequence of operations is the fire alarm designer’s; acceptance is the marshal’s. Wire the interface normally closed so a fault mutes and shows. Time the chain (T = Σ stage times) against the sequence. Never jumper, bypass or disable anything in it. Any change in the chain re-opens the test — so label the rack, lock the config, and make the next change visible.
